raw_comment: I can see that E-commerce is currently a booming industry within retail, and this stands out amongst the other forms of retail. While other forms of retail, including department stores and warehouse clubs, have remained largely the same in percentage change in jobs (graph B), E-commerce has been shooting up over the last decade and a half. I wonder the underlying causes of the steady decline of department stores, in particular. Overall, these graphs prove the common theme that our world is becoming increasingly technology-based and the new innovations that have arisen through this new world approach have far-reaching influences on our lives. Society is steadily shifting towards online commerce.

raw_comment: These graphs show an emergence of an industry that is like no other one before. It requires very little labor, but a lot of infrastruture. raw_comment:
I notice that the warehouse clubs had more jobs offered than the other commerce. E-commerce is the second most at offering jobs while department stores job offering declined. The total retail industry has increased from 2002 to 2008, but decreased until 2010. After 2010, the  job offerings increased rapidly increased. The other graph shows the percentage of job offering that each group offered over the 15 years. Although, e-commerce does not offer the most amount of jobs, it's percentage increased the most from 0 to 300% within the last fifteen years. I think what this may imply is that people are wanting to obtain better jobs because department stores don't offer as much money compared to warehouses and clubs. Since there's been significant increase in e-commerce, people are beginning to prefer working from home.

I wonder why the total retail industry declined from 2008 to 2010. Was there some sort mild depression that led to unemployment? Why are more jobs offered to warehouses and clubs rather than e-commerce? 

Not only do the people prefer to have better salary, warehouses, clubs and e-commerce require more people. Today, more people want to everything online, because it's cheaper, faster, and easier. That's why e-commerce has increased the most out of all other companies. I think e-commerce will eventually overtake warehouse/clubs employment, because of its rapid exponential progression.

raw_comment:
These 2 graphs show the change in retail jobs in America. The first one, however, shows the net change in retail jobs while the other shows the percent change. In the first graph the drastic change is more visible. Department stores have a less visible change in retail jobs, whereas retail jobs in warehous stores have been rapidly increasing. Additionally, ECommerce increases probably due to the prevalence of internet usage. The ECommerce shoppers most likely use it because it is more accessible and faster. 

I wonder whether the drastic decline in retail jobs around 2008 is due to a Stock Market Crash. Additonally, I wonder why warehouse stores have been receiving a large increasing. 

These graphs displays the rapidly changing industry and is representative of our constantly evolving world due to technology.

raw_comment:
These two different graphs show the transformation of retail jobs and department stores from 2002 to 2016. However, graph A reveals the net change of the jobs and stores, while graph B depicts the percentage change. The scales (y-axis) of the graphs are quite different, thus a clear comparison with distinct numbers will be unlikely.
The two graphs show a decrease of department stores; however, the rates of the decrease are significantly different. In graph A, the decrease is over 500 in some areas; while the graph B shows a general decrease a general of less than 100. Graph A shows a gradually increase of e- commerce, while graph B shows a faster one within the time frame. The large scale of graph A makes it very hard to decide how much the e- commerce has risen, while graph B shows a 300 increase.
There is a rise in the total retail industry on both graphs, but there is a very slight increase seen on graph B. The increase of the total industry of graph A was seen with a rise over 500,000. The same idea is presented in the rise of warehouse clubs and others.
These results are in response of new technology that allows one to buy ideas online much easier. I also believe that there is a need for jobs to be filled in existing department stores, before new one are built.

raw_comment:
As you look between the two graphs, you see a significant increase in both E-commerce and warehouses. I feel as though this is due to the extensive use of the internet in our modern day societies. With the growing of electronic ability, people tend to use their phone for more and more, including buying goods in which we have many sites including amazon, ebay, craigslist, etc. It was even shown that the number of people going out for black friday shopping significantly decreased from years prior and the number who participated in Cyber Monday skyrocketed. This increase of internet buying could be a factor to the disappearing department store.
The net change for the warehouse in the first graph was the greatest while the percentage of E-commerce is increasing more than the net change.

raw_comment:
Looking just at the first graph, I noticed that overall there has been an increase in the total amount of jobs in the retail industry. This shows that retail is gaining more consumer demand. There has been a gradual decrease in the amount of retail jobs at department stores. In the real world, some of the major department stores such as Sears are starting to go out of business. This implies that there is a trend of retail jobs shifting from department stores to online or warehouse clubs.
Looking at the second graph, I noticed that the E-commerce part of retail is exponentially increasing. This might be due to the growing popularity of online shopping and online delivery. The jobs at warehouse clubs are also increasing. The size of the retail industry has remained fairly constant, with years where they lost jobs and years it gained jobs. This implies that the retail industry is shifting away from department stores and toward the online forms of shopping. The ease and efficiency of online shopping has been increasing over the past few years. This can be seen by the growing size of the E-commerce side of the industry. I wonder why the warehouse clubs are gaining jobs?

raw_comment:
Both graphs illustrate the same general information, but Graph A depicts it via net change, using money by the thousands, which Graph B illustrates the percent change. This means that, while the data is the same, the depiction is wildly different; for instance, I notice that although warehouse clubs account for the largest amount of net chanege on the first graph, the percentage growth of e-commerce far exceeds that (even if it had less of a net change).

The story that these graphs are telling points to the increasingly shifting tides of retail as it orients away from department stores and more towards e-commerce. If the second graph is any indication, the retail industry isn't changing; it's the scope of it and the means of it that are changing its very definition. With that being said, I wonder how the continued growth of warehouse clubs can be explained; while not contradicting the observation of an increasing turn towards e-commerce, its continued survival raises some questions about the overall retail landscape.

raw_comment: On this graph it shows that E-commerce is becoming a very popular retail job and the department and warehouse stores are decreasing. It's not a surprise to me just because the internet is one of the biggest things that everyone is connected to. I personally would rather shop online just because I wouldn't have to waste my gas going to a store and deal with people, but I also would like to try on that piece of clothing or look at that certain item just to make sure it's to my liking. Society is steadily shifting towards online commerce.

raw_comment:
I notice that the warehouse clubs had more jobs offered than the other commerce. E-commerce is the second most at offering jobs while department stores job offering declined. The total retail industry has increased from 2002 to 2008, but decreased until 2010. After 2010, the  job offerings increased rapidly increased. The other graph shows the percentage of job offering that each group offered over the 15 years. Although, e-commerce does not offer the most amount of jobs, it's percentage increased the most from 0 to 300% within the last fifteen years. I think what this may imply is that people are wanting to obtain better jobs because department stores don't offer as much money compared to warehouses and clubs. Since there's been significant increase in e-commerce, people are beginning to prefer working from home.

I wonder why the total retail industry declined from 2008 to 2010. Was there some sort mild depression that led to unemployment? Why are more jobs offered to warehouses and clubs rather than e-commerce? 

Not only do the people prefer to have better salary, warehouses, clubs and e-commerce require more people. Today, more people want to everything online, because it's cheaper, faster, and easier. That's why e-commerce has increased the most out of all other companies. I think e-commerce will eventually overtake warehouse/clubs employment, because of its rapid exponential progression.

raw_comment:
These 2 graphs show the change in retail jobs in America. The first one, however, shows the net change in retail jobs while the other shows the percent change. In the first graph the drastic change is more visible. Department stores have a less visible change in retail jobs, whereas retail jobs in warehous stores have been rapidly increasing. Additionally, ECommerce increases probably due to the prevalence of internet usage. The ECommerce shoppers most likely use it because it is more accessible and faster. 

I wonder whether the drastic decline in retail jobs around 2008 is due to a Stock Market Crash. Additonally, I wonder why warehouse stores have been receiving a large increasing. 

These graphs displays the rapidly changing industry and is representative of our constantly evolving world due to technology.

These two different graphs show the transformation of retail jobs and department stores from 2002 to 2016. However, graph A reveals the net change of the jobs and stores, while graph B depicts the percentage change. The scales (y-axis) of the graphs are quite different, thus a clear comparison with distinct numbers will be unlikely.
The two graphs show a decrease of department stores; however, the rates of the decrease are significantly different. In graph A, the decrease is over 500 in some areas; while the graph B shows a general decrease a general of less than 100. Graph A shows a gradually increase of e- commerce, while graph B shows a faster one within the time frame. The large scale of graph A makes it very hard to decide how much the e- commerce has risen, while graph B shows a 300 increase.
There is a rise in the total retail industry on both graphs, but there is a very slight increase seen on graph B. The increase of the total industry of graph A was seen with a rise over 500,000. The same idea is presented in the rise of warehouse clubs and others.
These results are in response of new technology that allows one to buy ideas online much easier. I also believe that there is a need for jobs to be filled in existing department stores, before new one are built.

The ease and efficiency of online shopping has been increasing over the past few years. This can be seen by the growing size of the E-commerce side of the industry. I wonder why the warehouse clubs are gaining jobs?

raw_comment:
Both graphs illustrate the same general information, but Graph A depicts it via net change, using money by the thousands, which Graph B illustrates the percent change. This means that, while the data is the same, the depiction is wildly different; for instance, I notice that although warehouse clubs account for the largest amount of net chanege on the first graph, the percentage growth of e-commerce far exceeds that (even if it had less of a net change).

The story that these graphs are telling points to the increasingly shifting tides of retail as it orients away from department stores and more towards e-commerce. If the second graph is any indication, the retail industry isn't changing; it's the scope of it and the means of it that are changing its very definition. With that being said, I wonder how the continued growth of warehouse clubs can be explained; while not contradicting the observation of an increasing turn towards e-commerce, its continued survival raises some questions about the overall retail landscape.

raw_comment:
This graph is extremely important to understanding trends in our consumer economy over time. I notice that the graph shows a handful of left-skewed data that depicts the increase of net change and percent change of retail jobs in ECommerce, Warehouse clubs/other, Department Stores, and the Total Retail industry. Th e information in both graphs also suggests that each sector is showing increase in value except Department stores. It is also interesting to note that the Net Change and percent change of the total retail industry seems to have a pattern of increase and decrease in value. This could suggest that there was a shift in the demographic of sectors that make up the total retail industry; If a certain industry was the majority of retail for a certain time-period, it could have affected the entire net/ percent change of the retail industry. 

I wonder if this graph could further explain if parts of Total Retail have a larger influence on the consumer economy as a whole and if this is due to supply or demand. Is the lack of growth in Department store sales due to a preference for shopping and purchasing clothing online. What caused the initial dip in the value of E-Commerce? I wonder if this was due to skepticism among the participants.

From this graph, I can infer that the retail market is always shifting and depends on the creation of new and innovative forms of shopping and purchasing. The graph also serves as a representation of how competitive the industry is.

I noticed that there is a large increase in warehouses, while the number of department stores decrease.  There is also a large increase in E-commerce jobs, while the department stores are still decreasing.  

I wonder if there is a correlation between the increasing number of warehouses and E-commerce job increase to the declining number of department stores.  It might be because of the fact that people want to purchase items online and not in a physical store. 

These graphs illustrate the change in retail over the past 15 years.  It shows that our society uses and needs more jobs online, rather than physically. The graphs also show us that even though most retail jobs are decreasing, the E-commerce will need to hire more employees in order to run smoothly and efficiently.

raw_comment:
I notice the percentage change and net change in retail jobs over the past 15 years have changed according to each category of retail. Warehouse clubs/ other jobs and E- commerce have a sharp  positive slope while there is a decrease at a different consistency. Jobs in department stores have declined in popularity. In 2008, there was a stock market crash, shown on the graph with the plummeting decline. 

I wonder if the popularity of E- commerce will continue to increase, directly affecting department store retail negatively. I wonder which graph would be a better indicator of retail jobs generally, net change or percentage change.

The story the graph is telling is that the way people are utilizing retail methods is evolving; people are using alternative ways too shop (E- commerce) instead of in-store purchasing. It is easier, sometimes quicker to find what you are looking for, and cheaper. This affects and will continue to affect the economy due to less physical job opportunities.

raw_comment:
The first graph shows a change in retail jobs over the last 15 years, starting from 2002, while the second graph shows the change in percentage of retail jobs in the same sectors. The different industries shown are Department stores, E-commerce, and Warehouse Clubs and other. I also notice that jobs fro E-commerce and Warehouse Clubs and others has always increased, jobs for Departments stores has always decreased, and total retail jobs has been cyclical, initially starting off by increasing in jobs. This implies that the world is shifting to buying more in bulk and online.

I wonder why department store jobs has only decreased even though total retail jobs has increased tremendously over the past 7 years. I also wonder how E-commerce has increased so rapidly compared to other forms of retailers. This information could be found by doing research in the different fields and calculating total revenue earned by a single industry annually.

The story this graph is telling me is that the world, while it is transitioning to an ever-increasingly tech-based world, it is also shifting its consumption to online methods, notably Amazon.

By itself, department stores do not account for all of the decrease in the retail industry. There are actually many more sectors that are also losing their places to e-commerce.

raw_comment:
Between the two graphs I noticed that both warehouse clubs and E-Commerce retail have shown growth over the fifteen year period.  Department store jobs have shown a decrease from both graphs.  I'd expect the the large percent growth of jobs for E-commerce to be due to its rapid growth in modern society, and going from a relatively small number to a large one to accommodate the huge increase of people it needs to serve while the net change didn't seem so big in the grand scheme of things.  Would expect warehouse club net change to be so great because for each warehouse club kind of store, a lot of staff is needed which is why its change seems so much bigger.

I wonder if there is any correlation between the growth of E-Commrce jobs and the growth of jobs in warehouse clubs or if its coincidental.  I would also like to know what is driving up the need for positions in warehouse clubs.  E-commerce is hurting department stores due to convenience, but is the growth of warehouse clubs also affecting the decline in department stores?

The graph is showing the change in different retail services  over fifteen years.  The employment rate within warehouse clubs and E-commerce have grown a lot in net change and percent change respectively.  Also shows the decline of job growth in department stores, due to the growth of the other retail types.  Cool I guess...

raw_comment:
I noticed that in both graphs, there is a boom in the total number of jobs in the retail industry starting in 2012. There seems to be a correlation between the number of e-commerce jobs and total retail jobs because of a rapid growth in e-commerce, despite warehouse club jobs increasing at a steady rate. It also seems that the once prominent department store jobs have seen a decline over the years.

I wonder if said decline in department store jobs, as well as the decline in the net percent growth of the 25 other retail sectors, has to do with the growing popularity and accessibility of the e-commerce industry. It looks like the ease and lack of physical shopping e-commerce offers is the preferred alternative of society today. 

These graphs tell the story of e-commerce cultivating into its own convenient niche in the retail industry. While it provides a better alternative to department store chains that requires one to physically travel to shop, I do not believe e-commerce has grown to a point where it can render warehouse stores the inferior option. This seems to be partly due to the notion that when it comes to purchasing in bulk, there is a level of trust gained from purchasing packs of water or a large piece of furniture in person, rather than online where you cannot physically check for deficiencies on a larger scale.

raw_comment:
Looking at both the net and percentage change in retail jobs in the past 15 years, the most prominent feature is the positive slopes of E-commerce and Warehouse clubs/other jobs. It is clear that these positions are much more popular today than they were in 2002. I also notice the declining slope of department store jobs, indicating their decrease in popularity. Overall, the total retail industry has seen an increase since 2002, but has experienced intermittent decline (for example, in 2008 we see the slope plummet exponentially, likely due to the stock market crash of 2008). 

I can infer that the increasing number of retail positions in Ecommerce and Warehouse clubs is because of their increased utilization and popularity. Both online and in large stores, wide varieties of merchandise are available, easily accessible, and much cheaper than in department stores, making them the sought after option. Because online shopping and warehouse stores receive many customers and transactions, they require larger staffs to satisfy the needs of the store. The more successful they are, the more chains can be opened, hence increasing the workforce even further.  The recent unpopularity of department stores is likely due to people turning to these cheaper alternatives; hence, the more ecommerce and warehouse clubs dominate the retail industry, the more department store shopping will decline. Less traffic in department stores requires less staffing, and therefore, fewer jobs.

The story these graphs are telling is one of rapidly changing times that will exponentially follow this pattern.

Although overall the total retail industry has increased, it has fluctuated greatly. Department stores overall have significantly decreased.

Based on these observations, it is clear that E-commerce is changing the way shopping is occurring today, and this has a heavy impact in total retail industry as a whole. It is clear that department stores need to change their tactics if they want to be able to compete with E-commerce.

raw_comment:
I noticed that in both graphs, the net change and percentage change of retail jobs in department stores followed a negative slope. In contrast, E-commerce followed a positive slope. While the decrease in net and percentage change in department store retail jobs seems decrease at a more or less constant rate, E-commerce seems to increase almost exponentially with its greatest slope plotted between 2012 and 2016 on the percentage change graph. This may imply that there is a correlation between the increase and decrease in the two shopping methods. 

I wonder how much correlation there is between the increase in the net and percentage change in E-commerce and the decrease of department store net and percentage change. Are there any confounding variables that may inhibit causation or can one say that the drop in department store retail can be linked to the increase E-Commerce?

Based on my observations, I think these graphs show how E-commerce is quickly becoming the go-to shopping method. While warehouse retail and other clubs also proves to be a popular option, its net and percentage change of retail jobs increased at a fairly constant rate over the last 15 years while E-commerce spiked exponentially in the last 4. This spike in E-commerce percent change in jobs especially could be explained by the simplicity of online shopping that some people prefer.

raw_comment:
Thanks to all teachers and students who responded during this very busy time before vacation.  Did the graph make you want to shop for presents?

Many noticed that Graph A is the net change in jobs and Graph B is the percentage change.  Could you see how the net change was reflected in the percentage?  I think we were not surprised by the large increase in e-commerce jobs and corresponding large decrease in department store jobs.  But, we wondered whether this has affected sales.   And many wondered about the Warehouse graph. How did that coincide with the e-commerce jobs? Is there a connection between the two? Do we buy more or less with e-commerce?  What’s the future for retail jobs and sales? So many questions to consider.

Since we continue to post responses, whenever they arrive, is there more that you notice?  More that you wonder?  Talk to your classmates and even read the moderators’ responses.  Maybe something they say will lead to more things you notice, wonder, and conjecture.     

Remember to check back on Friday, December 15 to learn more about these graphs -- and we hope to see you again next month on Tuesday, January 9 (always the second Tuesday of the month) for our next "What's Going On In This Graph?"   Signing off now -- Sharon in Boston and Paul in Washington, DC.  See you next year!

What do you NOTICE? What may this imply?

What do you WONDER? Where could you find the answers to what you wonder?

What’s GOING ON in these graphs?  What can you infer that is beyond what the graphs show directly?

This month, we have two graphs.  Think about relating the graphs to each other to gain more insights.

Wouldn’t you love to hear what other students have to say about your response?  Read some responses.  Then, press "Reply" to an interesting response to get a discussion going.

We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Overall, the only change between the two graphs is that E-commerce has a higher percentage change than Warehouse clubs and other.
